t: valuations. A monetary consecration designated for the Temple. For some valuations the Torah fixes the amount to be given (valuations of persons, valuations of fields) and others are valued by their worth (houses, animals and movables), as will be explained.
vows of consecration. Vows of giving to the Temple (see Hilchot Nedarim 1:2).

when a man makes a special vow of the valuation of persons to the Lord. A man who utters with his lips ('yafli') a vow to consecrate to the Lord a valuation of persons ('be-erkekha nefashot la-Shem').

he shall not break. One who profanes his word and does not fulfill his vow transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated: 'When a man vows a vow to the Lord... he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that came out of his mouth' (Hilchot Nedarim 1:5).

you shall not delay. One who delays paying his vow to the Temple transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated: 'When you vow a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay paying it' (see Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 14:13).
he shall do according to all that came out of his mouth. This is a positive commandment, for every vow, that a person fulfill his vow (Hilchot Nedarim 1:4).
and it is a positive commandment to judge the laws of valuations as explained in the Torah. Leviticus 27:1-8, where the laws of valuations of persons are explained.
this valuation. This person.
according to the age of the one valued. According to the age of the person being valued.
and it is the fixed amount in the Torah. For the Torah fixed the sum of a person's valuation according to his age (Leviticus 27:3-7).
has no valuation. The Torah did not fix a valuation for him.
from time to time from the day of birth. Full years, from the date of birth until the same date in the following year (see also Hilchot Ishut 2:21).
a barley grain. A grain of barley (its weight is 1/20 gram).
and they already added to it and made it a sela. The Sages added to the weight of the Torah's shekel and adjusted it to the weight of the sela in their days.
as we explained in Hilchot Shekalim. 1:2.
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it cannot be determined whether he is male or female. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes this word 'tumtum'.]
and an androgynos. One who has both male and female organs, and the Sages did not decide whether he is treated as male or female (see Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25).
have no valuation. But they do value others (Mishnah Arakhin 1:1).
and likewise one who values a deaf-mute or an imbecile is liable. But they themselves do not value, because they lack understanding (Mishnah Arakhin 1:1).
the slave. A Canaanite slave who was circumcised and immersed for the sake of slavery, and who is in an intermediate status between a gentile and a Jew (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:11).

and if he is redeemed and has money, he gives the valuation he vowed. For the slave's money belongs to his master (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 2:8), and so the valuation he undertook remains on him as a debt until he is freed (for a similar law see Hilchot Hovel 4:21).
one afflicted with a skin disease. A person sick with a disease that causes limbs to fall off.
blind. Blind.
one-handed. Missing a hand.

the 'demim' (worth). A vow to give the Temple money equal to the worth of a certain person. Unlike valuations, the sum of the worth is not fixed by the Torah but is determined by the person's value as though he were sold as a slave (see also below, halakhah 23).
as if he were a slave sold in the market. Whose worth depends on his appearance, health and the like.

its unspecified use is for Temple maintenance. Money whose purpose was not explicitly stated is given for repair of the Temple and its needs. But if he specified its purpose, it is not given for Temple maintenance but for what he said (Me'iri on Arakhin; and see below 5:19).
and they shall fall. Shall be given.
for we do not accept from gentiles a freewill offering or vow to strengthen the Temple repairs or the repairs of Jerusalem. See also Hilchot Shekalim 4:8, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:8.
if he vowed with the intention of Israel. And he means that they decide what to do with this money.
the court uses it as seems fit to them. For example for charity or public need or other secular matters (Me'iri on Arakhin).
and if he said, I vowed to Heaven, it is hidden away. And likewise if he said nothing, for we suspect that perhaps he had Heaven in mind (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:8).
has no valuation and no worth. One cannot obligate oneself to the Temple for his valuation or his worth.

in a Jewish court to be put to death for a transgression he committed. But if he was sentenced by royal decree and the like, he has a valuation and worth because the king can change his mind (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 1:3).

any devoted thing that is devoted from man shall not be redeemed; he shall surely be put to death. Any consecration (devotion) of the valuation of a person condemned to death (to be devoted) need not be paid (redeemed), because he is sentenced to die.
and everything is collected from his property. Even if it passed to his heirs.

and a minor who has reached the age of vows. A boy from the age of thirteen years and a day, and a girl from twelve years and a day, even if they have not brought signs of maturity. From this age they are obligated to fulfill their vows (see Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-4, where it is explained that even before this age their vows may have effect).
as we explained in Hilchot Nedarim. 11:3.
his mouth and heart are equal. He means what he says with his mouth.
like other vows. See Hilchot Nedarim 2:2.
and they may be released. They may be annulled by a sage.
in the way that other vows and consecrations are released. Hilchot Shevuot chapter 6, Hilchot Nedarim 4:5-7.
one who says, the valuation of these is upon me. And he means a group of people who are before him.

the valuation of a poor person. A poor person does not give the full sum of the valuation but according to his means (see below 3:2-4), and in the case stated here he is obligated to give the valuation of a poor person for each of the people he valued, and he is not discharged by giving one poor person's valuation for all of them (Lechem Mishneh).
the valuation of a rich person. The full sum of the valuation fixed in the Torah.
is liable for each and every one. Just as a vow takes effect on top of a vow (Hilchot Nedarim 3:1-2), so a valuation takes effect on top of a valuation and he is obligated for each one separately.
gives the lowest of the valuations, which is three shekels. The valuation of a female from thirty-one days to five years (above halakhah 3).

and he shall stand him before the priest, and the priest shall value him. From this it follows that the one valuing must stand before the priest and only then is the obligation of the valuation fixed (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 5:2).
he stood trial and died. Even before the priest explicitly said what his valuation obligation is.

for valuations are fixed. Their sum is set and explicit in the Torah, and so the heirs are obligated by the mere standing of the person for judgment, even if the priest did not determine how much he must pay.
but worths are not fixed. And so standing for judgment is not sufficient, and the heirs' obligation to give them depends on determination of the value by ten, one of whom is a priest (as below 8:2).
and he died before his worth was assessed. The person vowed died before his value was determined.
every limb that, if removed from a living person, he would die. Since a person's life depends on this limb, it is considered as though he valued his entire body.

one who says, the worth of my head... gives the worth of the whole of him. For these are limbs on which a person's life depends, and it is as though he consecrated the value of the whole (as above halakhah 1 regarding valuations).
as he specified. And if he did not say explicitly, his law is detailed below, halakhah 7.
we see how much it is fit for a shekel. They weigh the hand.
the armpit. The underarm.
the knee-joint. The knee.

because in vows we follow the language of people. Although in various matters the word 'yad' (hand) refers to the palm and the word 'regel' (foot) refers to the foot down to the ankle (see Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 19b), in vows we interpret according to common usage among people (see Hilchot Nedarim 9:1).
a rod that does not bend to his full height. A thick pole that does not fold at the height of the one making the vow.
'my full height is upon me', he gives even a rod that bends. Since he added the word 'full', we interpret that he meant the measure of his height and not that the stick must stand as his height.
if he was very wealthy and intended a generous gift. His intention is interpreted according to his wealth and an estimate of his mind.
all these are doubtful. What he meant.

and he brings according to his wealth. According to his financial ability and an estimate of his mind we interpret his vow at its maximum, because in doubtful vows we are stringent (Hilchot Nedarim 9:4).

the heirs give the lowest of the meanings. Unlike the one who made the vow himself, for whom there is a doubt regarding the prohibition of 'he shall not break his word' and so the rule 'doubtful vows are treated stringently' applies, for the heirs there is only a monetary obligation and for them the rule 'a monetary doubt is treated leniently' applies, so they pay according to the minimal interpretation (Lechem Mishneh; see Kesef Mishneh, who explained otherwise).
he must give no less than a silver dinar. Which is the accepted coin of the silver type.

he must give no less than a silver ma'ah. Of copper worth a silver ma'ah, which is the smallest coin customarily traded, and he does not bring a copper perutah because it is not customary to trade in it due to its low value (Haggahot Ben Aryeh, Menachot 106b).
no less than a cubit by a cubit. Iron from which a sheet a cubit by a cubit in size can be made.

for 'kholah orev' that was above on the roof of the Sanctuary. On the parapet of the Sanctuary roof there was a pointed iron sheet so that birds would not rest on the roof of the Sanctuary, and 'kholah orev' means that it keeps ravens and the like from resting there.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Beit ha-Behirah 4:3.
tongue. A piece.
as we explained. Above 1:8.
secretly. In confidence and in hiding.
people of good standing. Respected and well-born people who are ashamed to receive charity openly.
to the Temple-repair chamber. Where the Temple-repair funds were kept.
for the altar's sacred things. For buying public offerings.
the terumah of the chamber. The half-shekel funds that were collected in the chamber and designated for buying public offerings (see Hilchot Shekalim 4:2).

they take out what is fit for them from the Temple-repair sacred things. Because the sanctity of the altar's needs is higher than the sanctity of Temple-repair needs, they bring out from a lesser sanctity to a greater sanctity.
they do not take out what is fit for them from the altar's sacred things. For we do not take out from a greater sanctity to a lesser sanctity.
less than twenty years old. Whose valuation is twenty shekels.
and did not stand for judgment. For the one valued must stand before the priest (as above 1:21).
that he be over twenty. Whose valuation is fifty shekels.
for the valuation is only at the time of the valuation. The valuation obligation takes effect at the time the person vowed, and it is fixed according to that.
and his means do not reach. He has no financial ability.
poor. Impoverished.
gives all that is found in his hand. Except certain things that are left to him, which will be detailed below, halakhot 14-18.
and is exempt. And is not obligated to complete the sum of the valuation even if he becomes rich afterward (below halakhah 7).

and all your valuation shall be in the shekel of the sanctuary. This means that a valuation of less than a shekel (sela) is not given, and so we learn that a poor person is discharged by giving a sela (Arukh ha-Shulchan 36:6).
all of it remains a debt on him. He remains liable for the full value of what he valued.
and the poor. Became poor after he valued.

he is liable for the valuation of a rich person. For anyone who was rich at the time he vowed the valuation or at the time of giving it is liable for a rich person's valuation (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 4:2).
he valued while poor and became rich and became poor again, he gives a poor person's valuation. Since he was poor both at the time he vowed the valuation and at the time of giving it.

what this one said is upon me. And by this statement he obligated himself in an obligation identical to what his fellow undertook, and both must bring a rich person's valuation (like the law of one who makes another's vow his own, Hilchot Nedarim 3:3).

what is the difference between one liable for a poor person's valuation and one liable for a rich person's valuation. What is the difference between a poor person who is liable for a poor person's valuation and a poor person who is liable for a rich person's valuation as explained at the beginning of halakhah 6, for in any case he does not have the means to pay the full worth of the valuation.

he is not judged by his means. Although he is poor, since he explicitly stated the worth of the valuation, the matter becomes a regular vow of consecration, in which we do not judge by financial ability.

'the worth of so-and-so is upon me' or 'the worth of so-and-so is upon me'. By this statement he obligates himself to the value of their worth as they would be sold as slaves in the market (as above 1:9).
one who says, 'a valuation is upon me' in general terms and did not specify. By this statement he is obligated to give the lowest valuation, three shekels (as above 1:20).
one who says, 'my valuation is upon me' and again says 'my valuation is upon me'. By this statement he undertook two valuations (as above 1:19).
and he had ten sela in his hand. Ideally he should give the ten sela for the first valuation, and the second valuation remains on him as a debt.

and gave nine for the second and a sela for the first, he has fulfilled his obligation. When he paid the second valuation first, although at the time of payment a sela remained in his hand, he is considered to have given all that his means reached, since the remaining sela is pledged for the first valuation. And when he later pays the remaining sela for the first valuation, he has also fulfilled the obligation of that valuation.

that valuations are not like debts... a consecrated item, once collected, is collected. In an ordinary monetary debt, if the second creditor was first and collected his debt, what he collected is taken from his hand and brought to the first creditor (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 20:1), but with consecrated property, if he paid his second debt first, what he paid is not taken back for the sake of the first debt.
therefore the rest of the first valuation remains on him. By the law of one who did not give all his means reach, who has not fulfilled his valuation obligation.
one who says, 'two valuations of mine are upon me'. And he immediately obligated himself in two separate valuations.

even if he did not say 'upon me'. For example he said 'I am in my valuation' or 'I am in the valuation of so-and-so' (Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 139a), for if he said 'upon me' he is certainly liable for its safety like other vows (Hilchot Nedarim 1:2).
is liable for its safety. And he must pay it.
until they reach the treasurer's hand. And after they reach the treasurer he is not liable for their safety.
they are seized by pledge and what they vowed is taken from them against their will. Things belonging to them are taken as a pledge, or as payment for the valuation they vowed.

and they are not obligated to return the pledge by day or by night. Unlike a creditor who takes a pledge from a borrower, who must return the pledge when he needs it (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:5). Apart from this difference, the collection laws for one obligated to the Temple are similar to those of an ordinary loan (ibid. 1:4-7).
that he dyed for them... that he bought for them. That he dyed or bought for his wife and children, even though they have not yet actually worn them.
and likewise one who consecrates all his property. One who undertakes to give all his property to the Temple (see below 6:3).
they give him tefillin. But if he consecrated all his property, they do not give him his tefillin (below 6:3).
and a mat. A reed mat on which a poor person customarily sleeps.
even though he is obligated for their sustenance and clothing. See Hilchot Ishut 12:2, 12:14, 13:6.
for weekdays. For ordinary days.
craftsman. A tradesman.
carpenter. A woodworker.
planes. Tools for smoothing and leveling wood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 6:2).
saws. Saws.
and few of the second kind. One tool.

they do not sell from the many and buy for him from the few. Although one could say that he usually lends out some of the many tools and receives in return from the few kind, and now that he will be left with only two of the many kind and one of the few kind they will no longer lend to him because of his poverty, this is not taken into account (ibid. 6:4).

they do not give him his animal, even though he has no sustenance except from it. Because the animal and the ship are defined as property even if he earns his living from them (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 1:7).
the merchants. The traders.
it would improve by a hundred. Its value would rise by a hundred dinars.
for the market day. The market day.
would improve by ten. Its value would rise by ten dinars.
we do not listen to them. To delay the sale and invest in improving the items.
they beautify. They adorn.
for we do not beautify it etc.. Because the profits expected from these actions are not certain and it could cause the Temple a loss (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 6:5).
but land. Which does not spoil like movables and slaves.
they announce it for sixty consecutive days. Thereby many people hear about the land and raise its price.
morning and evening. These are the hours when workers gather before going out to work and after returning from work (see below 4:27, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 12:8).

a field of inheritance. The law of a field of inheritance applies only in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Bikkurim 1:6), and only when the tribes dwell on their inheritance and the Jubilee is in force (Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 10:9, below 5:1).
that he bought. That he acquired.
or acquired. As a gift or from ownerless property.
they measure it. To determine the price of its redemption.
and its valuation. The price of its redemption.
the fixed valuation in the Torah. Leviticus 27:16.

any place fit for sowing a chomer of barley etc.. An area in which a chomer measure of barley grain is sown, by hand-scattering and leaving a medium gap between the seeds (below, halakhah 4, the length measure of this area is explained).

fifty shekels for every two jubilees. This is the full sum in the case of redemption in the forty-ninth year, for example if he redeems immediately after the Jubilee. And if the field is redeemed later, the sum is reduced proportionally, as below, halakhah 5.
in this way they value it. For the Torah fixed a set valuation for fields without regard to the quality of the field, like valuations of persons (above 1:8).
in Hilchot Shekalim. 1:2-3.
and the gerah mentioned in the Torah. For example in the passage on valuations: 'twenty gerahs to the shekel' (Leviticus 27:25).

and they added to the shekel and made it a sela. They added to the weight of the Torah's shekel, whose value was twenty gerah and weight three hundred twenty barley grains, and adjusted it to the weight of the sela in their days, whose weight was three hundred eighty-four barley grains.
and the ma'ah is two pundyonim. So the sela is forty-eight pundyonim.

it turns out that for each year it is a sela and a pundyon. For the full valuation for each sowing of a chomer of barley is fifty sela, and when we divide it into forty-nine years one must give for each year a sela plus one forty-ninth of a sela, and when he gives a sela and a pundyon for each year he gives fifty sela and a pundyon.
for although the sela is forty-eight pundyon. So it turns out that he gave one extra pundyon unnecessarily.

when he gives pundyonim, he takes a sela from the money-changer and gives forty-nine. One who converts pundyonim to a whole sela gives the money-changer (shulchani) an additional pundyon as an exchange fee. Against this fee (which the treasurer would have to give when he converts the pundyonim he received), the Sages added one pundyon to the total sum when one redeems from the Temple (see also Hilchot Shekalim 3:1).
in Hilchot Shabbat. 16:3.
in its area. In its surface.
of a se'ah's sowing. A place where a se'ah is sown.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 2.
because they add a fifth. As stated in the Torah: 'And if he who consecrated the field will redeem it, he shall add a fifth of the money of your valuation to it' (Leviticus 27:19).
they give a fifth. Five sela and five pundyonim, since they add a fifth (some versions read: 'they give a chomesh').
rather he gives it all together. He gives the whole sum in a single payment, not the payments of each year separately.
with a deduction of money. A deduction from the full sum according to the count of years as above.
to count the months as a year. To count them as a full year, and so he can redeem the field at the valuation of two years.

because we do not count months for consecrated property. And so the sum cannot be reduced according to the number of months he used the field, but either they count them as a full year or he redeems at the full sum, as the treasurer wishes.

therefore it is not fitting for a person to consecrate his field etc.. It is not advisable to consecrate a field less than two years before the Jubilee, because it depends on the treasurer's wish, and he might not allow the redeemer to pay only the valuation of two years, and he would have to pay the full sum of fifty sela for each sowing of a chomer of barley.
and it is not redeemed with a deduction of money. Unless the treasurer wishes, as above.
as will be explained. Below, halakhah 19.
just as they redeem forever. The priest and the Levite may redeem the field even after the Jubilee year, as below, halakhah 21.
so they consecrate forever. Even in the Jubilee year itself.
because we do not count months for consecrated property. And the months he used the field cannot be deducted from the sum.
when they measure. The field, to calculate its value according to its size.
they are not measured with it. And there is no need to give anything to the Temple for their redemption.
they are measured by themselves and they calculate for them what is proper. According to the calculation of valuations of fields (see Piskim ve-Shittot).
even though he did not specify. That he did not explicitly consecrate the trees.

for anyone who consecrates does so generously. And so we interpret that his intention was to consecrate the trees by themselves, and not that the trees be redeemed along with the land, as he goes on to explain (Lechem Mishneh).
as we explained. Above, halakhah 5.
rocky ground. Hard, stony land.
they redeem it at its value. And not by the calculation of valuations of fields.
the trees were. When he consecrated the trees.

he has consecrated the land. Because this spacing is fit for a tree field (see Hilchot Shemittah 3:2), it is understood that his intention was for the trees and for the land they grow in. He must redeem the trees at their value and the land by the calculation of valuations of fields (as above, halakhah 15).
and the trees among them. Small trees between the large trees.
any three trees in more than a beit se'ah or less. This is not the spacing fit for a tree field, and so the land is not included in the consecration of the trees.
or he consecrated them one after another. Although there were three within a beit se'ah, because he consecrated each one separately, the land was not consecrated with them.
the priests. Of that watch in which the Jubilee fell (as below, halakhah 24).
as we explained. Above, halakhah 19.
the priests need not give the price. Referring to the end of the previous paragraph, when the field becomes a holding of the priests.
it is a doubt whether it returns to the woman. By the law of a son who redeemed his father's field.
or goes out to the priests. By the law of other relatives who redeemed the field.
it is given to the priests of the watch in which the Jubilee fell. By giving its price for its redemption, as above, halakhah 19.

to the priests of the watch in which the Jubilee fell. The priests were divided into twenty-four groups called watches, and each week a different watch served in the Temple, and the changing of the watches was on Sabbath (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:3).
how much it is worth until the Jubilee. For in the Jubilee it returns to its first owners.
he does not add a fifth. Unlike one who consecrated a field of inheritance, who must add a fifth when he redeems it (as above, halakhah 5).
and it goes out in the hand of another. It goes out to the owners from the hand of the one who redeemed it from the Temple.
for a person does not consecrate what is not his. And it does not belong to the buyer who consecrated it, for it returns in the Jubilee to the first owners.
to sell it for its value. According to its worth, such as a purchased field or a rocky field.
at the time workers are brought in. To work, so that the householder may ask them whether they have examined the field offered for redemption.
at the time workers are sent out. At the end of the work, so that he may ask them to examine the field offered for redemption.
and they mark its boundaries. They mark the field's borders.
so good is it. They describe the quality of the yield and the like.
and for this it is appraised; whoever wishes to buy, let him come and buy. They announce at what sum they appraised its value, and the field is given to the highest bidder.
the buyer. The purchaser.
and whether he consecrated it in the lifetime of his father or the one who bequeathed to him, and afterward his father died. And at the time he consecrated it he had not yet inherited it.
his field of inheritance. A field he received by inheritance (as above 4:1).

it is a commandment upon him to redeem it himself. The Sages learned this from the verse on redeeming an unclean animal, 'and if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at your valuation' (Leviticus 27:27), that if it is not redeemed by the owners it is sold to anyone, and from this, that the master has priority (Mishnah Bekhorot 1:7).
at a time when the commandment of the Jubilee is in force. When the Temple stands and all the tribes are in the Land, each tribe on its inheritance (Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 10:8).

for if the Jubilee comes and he does not redeem it, it goes out to the priests. So there is no need for compulsion, for if he does not redeem it himself he will lose his field. And the Temple does not lose, for when it goes out to the priests they will give its price (Radbaz).
as we explained. Above 4:19.

but at a time when the jubilees have ceased etc.. Here it speaks of a time when the Temple stands and the redemption money goes to Temple repairs, and see below 8:10 for the law of redeeming consecrated items when the Temple does not stand.

we compel the owner to open first. Because he adds a fifth, and because the commandment is on the owner, and because it is dearer and more desirable to him than to another person (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 8:1).
to open. To propose a price for its redemption.
and it is redeemed at its value like other consecrated items. For when the Jubilee is not in force one does not redeem by the calculation of valuations of fields.
it is yours. The field is yours for your offer.
he has priority over everyone. Even in these cases where redemption depends on his wish and he is not commanded to redeem.

which is not so with one who sells to a layman. That he is forbidden to sell or borrow in order to redeem, and he does not redeem in halves (Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 11:17-18). The reason is that with a consecrated field of inheritance, if he does not redeem it, it does not return to its owner, so the Torah was lenient about its redemption (Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 30b).
adds a fifth. Adds a fifth part, equal to a quarter of the principal sum (as above 4:5).
in houses of walled cities. Cities surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun.
from houses of the villages. Cities that are not walled.

it is redeemed forever. Unlike one who sells a house in a walled city to his fellow, where if he did not redeem it within twelve months of the sale the house is permanently acquired by the buyer (for details of these laws see Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 12:1-4).
one redeemed it from the Temple etc.. See also Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 12:8.

if it was a house in a walled city and it remained in the redeemer's hand twelve months, it is permanently acquired. By the law of one who buys a house in a walled city from his fellow, that if its owner did not redeem it within twelve months, it is permanently acquired by the buyer (ibid.).
it returns to its owner in the Jubilee. By the law of one who sells a house in the villages, that even if he did not redeem it, it returns to its owner in the Jubilee (ibid. 12:10).
unblemished. Without a blemish, fit for offering on the altar.
that he transgressed a positive commandment. As explained in the next halakhah.
and it is redeemed while unblemished. And one need not wait for a blemish to occur in it (unlike an animal that was consecrated for the altar, which is not redeemed without a blemish).
for what it is fit. For the offering for which it is fit to be offered, such as a male for an olah and the like.

for anything fit for the altar never leaves the altar's ownership. And therefore the sanctity of the body applies to it and it does not become secular by being redeemed, although it was consecrated not to the altar but for Temple repairs.
sarua and kalut. Two types of blemished animals, which may not be offered (see Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash 7:9, Hilchot Issurei Mizbeach 2:5).
from the oral tradition. The Sages' tradition in interpreting the verses.

and likewise the matters show that it is only sanctity of value. Even from the plain sense of the verse it is reasonable that it speaks of a donation of money and not a donation to the altar, for a blemished animal is not fit for the altar.
you make it a freewill offering for Temple repairs. Specifically when it is blemished.

and a prohibition derived from a positive commandment is like a positive commandment. A prohibition learned from the category of a positive commandment is not considered a negative prohibition but a positive commandment.
one who consecrates... in general terms. And did not specify whether he consecrates for Temple repairs or for the altar.
the males are sold to those who need olot. People who need to bring an olah offering.
and the females are sold to those who need shelamim. For a female is not offered as an olah.

and the proceeds fall to Temple repairs, for general consecrations are for Temple repairs. And we do not say that the animals were consecrated for the altar and must be offered as freewill olot on the altar (males) or that olot for the altar be bought with their proceeds (females).

and about this it is said... whatever is fit to be offered on the altar shall be offered. Therefore, although he consecrated them for Temple repairs, one must ensure that the animal itself is offered on the altar.
wines, oils and fine flours. Which are fit for libations of offerings or for a meal offering of libations.
are sold to those who need that kind. To those who need to bring an offering or libations of these kinds.
and with the proceeds males are bought and offered as olot. Freewill olot for the altar.

because an animal consecrated to the altar, if a blemish occurs in it, has redemption, as will be explained. Below, halakhah 11, that through redemption the sanctity passes to the money and one buys another animal for the offering. For this reason, when the donor's animal is sold for an offering and the altar's obligation is thereby fulfilled, the animal's proceeds may go out to Temple repairs. But with these items, since they have no redemption, even when sold for the altar's purposes the obligation of offering on the altar remains on their proceeds, and they cannot go out to Temple repairs.

as it is stated, 'and he shall stand the animal before the priest' etc.. From this, only the animal about which the verse explicitly says that it is stood and valued is redeemed, but not other things that were consecrated to the altar (Radbaz, Hilchot Issurei Mizbeach 6:4; Arukh ha-Shulchan, Kodashim 60:11). Some explain that this refers specifically to things with a living spirit that can be stood before the priest, unlike flour, wine and oil, and birds are included here, since they do not stand but fly with their wings (Keren Orah, Menachot 100b; Hidushei ha-Rambam [ed.], Menachot 12:1).
and it included incense that is given to craftsmen as their wages until they return and take it. For example, the one who consecrated was a craftsman who received incense as his wages.

as we explained in Shekalim. 4:12. That in the month of Nisan they would redeem the surplus incense from the previous year with the wage money of the incense craftsmen taken from the chamber, and give the incense to the craftsmen as wages, and afterward would buy the incense from them with the shekels of the new terumah.

it is given to the craftsmen as their wages. And it cannot be sold so that the buyer would give it to the Temple, and its proceeds fall to Temple repairs, since an individual does not bring incense as a freewill offering (Radbaz).

is valued and redeemed. Its value is assessed and its sanctity is transferred to the money. And it is a positive commandment to redeem a sacrificial animal that has developed a blemish (Hilchot Issurei Mizbeach 1:10).
and if any unclean animal. And the Sages explained that the verse speaks of a blemished animal.
rather it is buried. Because it is forbidden to derive benefit (Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 19:1).
consecrated a slaughtered animal or a carcass for Temple repairs. Or for the altar (Kesef Mishneh).

both altar-sacred animals that developed a blemish. After they were consecrated (as above, halakhah 11). But one who consecrates an animal with a permanent blemish, it needs no standing and valuation, and even if it died before being redeemed, it is redeemed after it dies (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbeach 1:10-11).

or an unblemished one fit to be offered as explained. Above, halakhot 5-7, that when he consecrated it for Temple repairs, it is redeemed at its price while unblemished and sold to be offered for what it is fit.
standing in judgment. For monetary valuation.
it is not redeemed after it died. Because it is not fit for standing in judgment.
slaughtered two or the majority of two. The two signs of slaughter, which are the windpipe and the gullet.
convulsing. Twitching.
it is like a live one for all its matters. Although for eating it is considered a valid slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 3:5), nevertheless for standing and valuation it is considered alive.
one who consecrates an unblemished animal for its value. That he bring an offering for the altar with its proceeds.

its body is consecrated. Although he consecrated it for its value, since it is unblemished and fit for the altar the sanctity of the body applies and it does not leave the altar's ownership (as above, halakhah 5).

they sell it entire to one who will offer it, and its proceeds are secular except the price of that limb. For example, the buyer vowed to bring an offering of a certain cost, and after deducting the price of that limb this animal is worth the cost he vowed (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 15:2).
a limb on which life depends. That the animal's life depends on its existence, such as the heart and the like.
the sanctity spread to all of it. And it is considered as though he consecrated all of it for its value.
only the price of that limb alone was sanctified. Since the animal is not fit for the altar, the sanctity does not spread to all of it, even if he consecrated a limb on which life depends.

he and the Temple are partners in it. In the price of that limb. Therefore when he consecrated a limb on which life depends, he and the Temple are partners in the price of the entire animal and divide its price. Whereas when he consecrated a limb on which life does not depend, he gives the Temple the price of that limb (Radbaz).
and likewise one who says etc.. The law stated above regarding consecration of a blemished animal for its value applies also where he consecrated an unclean animal or a slave for its value.

he is liable only for the worth of its head. Since the sanctity does not spread to all of it, only its head is consecrated, and since its head is a limb on which life depends, he and the Temple are partners in it and divide its price.

and we see how much that limb would be worth if sold. Therefore when he consecrated a limb on which life depends he gives half to the Temple, like one who sold his fellow the head of a slave or a donkey, who has sold him half of it (see Hilchot Mekhirah 27:8).

in what case does this apply, with altar-sacred things. That when they are not fit for the altar and he consecrated them for their value, the sanctity does not spread through the whole animal, but he is liable only for the price of that limb.
for all Temple-repair consecration is sanctity of value. And anyone who values or consecrates a limb on which life depends has the law of one who values or consecrates the whole body (above 2:1).
it is a doubt whether he is judged by means. By the law of a poor person who made a valuation (above 3:2-3).
they redeem it at the fixed valuation in it. By the law of a field of inheritance valuation (above 4:1-2).
or they redeem it at its value since he consecrated it for the altar. And we have not found anything consecrated for the altar that is not redeemed at its true value (Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 5a).
to be stringent. If the valuation is more than the value, he gives the valuation. And if the value is more than the valuation, he gives the value.
cherem. A term meaning removal of something from a person's possession.
these go to the priests. They are given to the priests who were on duty at the time he declared the cherem (as below, halakhah 5).

and from his Canaanite slaves and families. Whose bodies are owned by him. But he cannot declare a cherem on a Hebrew slave or maidservant because their bodies are not owned by him (as below, halakhah 21).
of all that he has. And not all that he has.

they take everything he has etc.. Although when seizing those liable for valuations and worths they leave them tefillin and some of the tools of their trade (above 3:14-18), here, with one who consecrates all his property, they take everything that belongs to him except his family's clothing (ibid. halakhah 14).
like terumah. Which is not redeemed. But once they reach the priest's hand, laymen may derive benefit from them (below, halakhah 5).
to the priest of that watch. See above 4:24 and the explanation.
a cherem field. A field he acquired from a cherem.

that he acquired after the Jubilee. This language is difficult, since there seems to be no connection between the Jubilee and the priest's acquisition of the cherem field. Some emended it to 'or that he acquired after the Jubilee' (Kiryat Sefer; Arukh ha-Shulchan 40:19), and according to this emendation there is an additional case here, referring to a field of inheritance that was not redeemed and went out to the priests at the Jubilee, and this priest acquired it and now declared it a cherem (as above 4:19; see Tzafnat Pa'ne'ach there, who resolved Rambam according to the text before us).

this teaches that his cherem field is for him like a field of inheritance for an Israelite, that if he declares it a cherem it is under cherem. Just as an Israelite can declare a cherem on his field of inheritance, so the priest can declare a cherem on this field that he acquired (but the priest's own field of inheritance he cannot declare cherem, as explained in the next halakhah).
his cherem field. A field he acquired from the cherem.
and the buyer consecrated it. The buyer consecrated the field.
like a purchased field. That returns to the first owners at the Jubilee (as above 4:26).
and it returns to the priest who sold it in the Jubilee. Since he acquired it from the cherem, he is defined as its owner.

but land or movables of priests and Levites, they do not declare cherem on them. Unlike what was said in the previous halakhah, that a priest can declare a cherem on a cherem field he acquired, priests cannot declare cherem on their own lands, and the same law applies to their movables (but in the language of consecration they can consecrate their fields, as above 4:21 - Tzafnat Pa'ne'ach 4:19). Some explain that this law concerns only priestly cherem, that priests and Levites cannot make their land and movables into priestly cherem, but they can declare them cherem for the Most High (Minchat Chinuch 357, Arukh ha-Shulchan 40:16-17, Likkutei Halakhot, Arakhin 28a).
altar-sacred things. An animal that was consecrated for offering on the altar.

the consecration takes effect on them. Although the animal's body is consecrated to the altar, the consecration takes effect on the monetary right the owners have in it, and so he must pay its value to Temple repairs (as detailed below, halakhot 11-12).
consecrated item. For Temple repairs.
it is permitted for benefit. For the consecration has not yet taken effect (and it is also permitted to eat, see Hidushei ha-Rambam, Temurah 3:1).
he consecrated it to the altar. Within the thirty days.
from now, after thirty days. For after thirty days the consecration takes effect retroactively from the time of the statement.
it is forbidden for benefit. For the consecration has taken effect on it, and when it is dead he cannot stand it, value it and redeem it (as above 5:12).
it is not consecrated. For a person does not consecrate what is not his (as above 5:8).

there is only a holding by the treasurers. Although he must pay its value to Temple repairs (as above 5:8), the payment does not hold up the slaughter; rather the treasurers hold up its offering to assess its value in order to obligate the one who consecrated it (as explained in the following halakhot).
both priestly cherem and Temple-repair cherem. He can declare as cherem most-holy or lesser-holy offerings for both these types of cherem.
sacred things for whose safety he is liable. For example if he said 'an olah is upon me' and set aside an animal for his olah, so that if it died or was stolen he must bring another animal.
he gives their value. Since he is liable for its safety, the offering is considered his, and he must redeem it by giving its value.
they were a freewill offering. For example if he said 'this is an olah', and if it died or was stolen he need not bring another animal.

how much a person would be willing to give for this animal to offer it as an olah that he is not obligated to bring. This is the benefit the consecrator has in this animal, for if the animal died or was stolen he would be exempt from bringing another for the offering, but he would lose the opportunity of bringing an olah, and the cherem takes effect on the value of this benefit.
whether it was unblemished or blemished. In both cases the Israelite must give it to the priests (Hilchot Bekhorot 1:1-3), and the cherem takes effect on the Israelite's benefit, as follows.
to give for this firstborn. To pay for the purchase of the firstborn.
the tithe. The animal tithe, which is not given to the priests but is eaten entirely by its owners (Hilchot Bekhorot 6:4).
like one who declares cherem on freewill peace offerings. As above, halakhah 12.

it is sacred. For he is liable for its safety until it reaches the treasurer's hand (Hilchot Shekalim 3:8), and so the sanctity of Temple repairs takes effect on it as a freewill offering and he gives its value (as above, halakhah 11).

consecrated bikkurim for Temple repairs, they are not sacred. Because they belong to the priests, and a person does not consecrate what is not his (as above 5:8; Tosafot Yom Tov and Tiferet Yisrael, Shekalim 8:8).
these are sacred. For they are the priest's property (Hilchot Bikkurim 4:14).
the one who declares cherem. For the priests.

he and the priests are partners in it. Because priestly cherem items are sacred only until they come to the priest's hand and afterward become secular in his hand, there is no sanctity here that would spread through the whole body of the slave or maidservant (Arukh ha-Shulchan 42:5). The remedy for such a slave is that the master give him as a gift in order to return him to the priest, and the priest use him one day and the master one day, or the priest give half the slave's value to his master and the slave be given to the priest (Hidushei ha-Rambam, Arakhin 4:11).
all of him is sacred as we explained. Above 5:18, that one who consecrates for Temple repairs a limb on which life depends is liable for the price of the whole.
until they are redeemed. That they be sold to others, and their price given to Temple repairs.

and the treasurers are not permitted to take their price from others and take them out to freedom. So that it not be said that the treasurers treat Temple money lightly, but in a sale they are more careful to sell them at their value and there is no such concern (Tosafot, Gittin 38b).
one who consecrates the work of his slave's hands. And he means the product of the slave's hands.

borrows, eats, works and repays. He borrows money from others for his food, and afterward does work for less than a perutah's worth so that the consecration not take effect, and pays back the loan little by little.

less and less than a perutah's worth. Since the master's monetary right in the product of his slave's hands is only to the value of a perutah, he cannot consecrate except from a perutah's worth and up (Meiri, Gittin 12b).
he consecrated only his value. He is assessed as a slave sold in the market, and he gives it to Temple repairs (as above 1:9).
his purchased field. Although he can consecrate it, it is destined to return to its owner in the Jubilee and it is not under cherem forever (as above 4:26).
for a person does not consecrate what is not his. And the bodies of his Hebrew son and daughter or male and female slave are not owned by the father or master.
if he can extract it through legal proceedings. If he has the ability to win the field back with the help of the court.

for the land itself is in its owner's possession. Because 'land cannot be stolen' - it is always defined as in its owner's presumptive possession and a robber has no acquisition or possession in the stolen land (Hilchot Gezelah 8:14).
it is as though he fixed a price. As though he named a price for each gourd or egg.
for it is not in his possession. For when the buyer takes something of fixed price, he acquires it by lifting and it passes to his possession (Hilchot Mekhirah 4:11-12).
my fishing net. The net he spread in the sea.
he said nothing. Since nothing has yet come up in his net and his produce has not yet grown.
she works and eats and the surplus is secular. Because her work has not yet come into the world, and a person does not consecrate something that has not come into the world.
to their makers. To the Holy One, blessed be He, who made them.

since they are pledged to him, all the work of her hands is sacred. For the Sages enacted that a woman's handiwork belongs to her husband (Hilchot Ishut 12:3; see also Hilchot Nedarim 12:10), and since her hands exist in the world, this is not defined as something that has not come into the world.
this field that I pledged to you. As security for a loan.
when I redeem it. When I repay the loan.
even if it was pledged for a fixed time. And he cannot take it back now.
and then consecrated it again. The lessor.
it is sacred and the lease is cancelled. Although the field is pledged to the lessee, the consecration removes it from the lien, as below (7:14).
misappropriated. Derived forbidden benefit from consecrated property, and must pay principal plus a fifth to the Temple and bring a guilt offering for misappropriation (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3).
like other vows. Hilchot Nedarim 1:4-5, and see also above 1:1.
what our father Jacob said etc.. And at the time he vowed he had no property in his hand.
he must become a nazirite. Immediately, lest he die now (Hilchot Nezirut 1:4); so although he did not take nazirite status upon himself, he is obligated in it because of a vow.

he made another apply by it and said 'this one like this one', the second is consecrated. The commentators found Rambam's words difficult here, for the consecration did not take effect on the first, so how could he make sanctity apply to the second animal through it. Some explained that the application of sanctity to the second was done before he learned of the error in the consecration of the first, and so the sanctity applied by virtue of the principal consecration that exists here (see Radbaz here and in Responsa Radbaz 5, no. 1448; see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh, who explained in other ways).
they are not redeemed. One does not pay in exchange for them to take them out to secular status.
for they were likened to land. They were equated with it halakhically, as learned from the verse 'and you shall bequeath them to your children' (Leviticus 25:46, Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
for their bodies are not money. They have no monetary value, but serve only as proof of a monetary obligation.
as it is stated, 'and he shall give the money'. See below, halakhah 12 and the explanation.
bran. The husks of wheat grains after milling, whose value is very low.
adds a fifth. An addition of a quarter of the principal (as above 4:5).
as we explained. Above 5:3.

and the fifth that he adds is like the consecrated item itself and they have one law. That one commits misappropriation with it, and if he redeems the fifth from the Temple, he adds a fifth to its redemption (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:5; unlike the second consecration explained below, halakhah 4, on which he does not add a fifth).
and by rabbinic enactment. By the words of the Sages.
they permitted him to eat. Consecrated items were permitted for eating.

and the treasurers are demanding it from him. The Temple treasurers will demand the money from him on a weekday, and so, together with this reason, they permitted it for the sake of Sabbath delight (Kesef Mishneh; compare Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:12).
altar-sacred animals that developed a blemish and were redeemed. As above 5:11.

not the one who gets atonement through it who redeemed it. For example, a person vowed to bring an offering and his fellow set aside the offering for him; the one who vowed himself does not add a fifth to its redemption, but only the consecrator himself when he redeems.
and the first consecration. Something that was secular and he consecrated it at the outset.

second consecration. Something to which sanctity passed by virtue of another thing that was consecrated and redeemed (for example one who consecrates an animal and after it was disqualified redeemed it on another animal; if he comes to redeem the second, he does not add a fifth).

the one who consecrates, not the one who applies. The addition of a fifth applies specifically when he redeems the thing that was secular and that he consecrated at the outset, and not an item to which sanctity passed by virtue of other sanctity.
desecrated. Redeemed.
or exchanged in altar-sacred animals. He said of a secular animal that it be sacred in exchange for the first animal, in which case both are sacred (see Hilchot Temurah 2:2).
when he redeems the second on which he desecrated. For example if a blemish occurred in it.
and desecrated it on another animal. In order to offer it as a guilt offering and gain atonement through it.
and was atoned through another guilt offering. For example the second animal was lost, and he brought another for the guilt offering and afterward the second animal was found.

and the animal on which he desecrated was removed to grazing. The second animal was removed from the law of a guilt offering to the law of grazing until a blemish occurs in it and it is redeemed, and its proceeds go to a freewill olah offering.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 4:14.
it is a doubt whether he adds a fifth to it. When he redeems it after a blemish occurred in it.
since it is an olah offering. For by strict law the animal itself is fit for an olah and not only its proceeds are offered as an olah (see ibid. halakhah 15).

and it is another body and another sanctity. It is not the original offering in which the blemish occurred but another animal, and likewise it is offered not as a guilt offering but as an olah, and for these reasons it should not be defined as second consecration but as first consecration (Lechem Mishneh; see Kesef Mishneh, who read and explained it differently).
Temple-repair consecrated things do not take exchange. And if he exchanged for them, the sanctity does not take effect on the substituted animal (Hilchot Temurah 1:12).
'this is in exchange for this' or 'this is a substitute for this', he said nothing. For these expressions are expressions of temurah.

'this is in place of this'. This expression can serve for temurah and can serve for redemption, and its meaning depends on context (see ibid. 2:3), and when he used this expression regarding Temple-repair consecrated things, since they are not exchanged, we interpret that he meant redemption.
or 'this desecrates on this'. Which is not an expression of temurah but of redemption (ibid. 1:1).

and the first animal went out to secular status. Specifically where a blemish occurred in this animal, but if no blemish occurred in it, unblemished Temple-repair consecrated animals never leave the altar's ownership (as above 5:5).
investigation of the price. Examining the value of the consecrated item before redemption, so that it be redeemed at the appropriate value (as below, halakhah 11).
and he must complete its price. In a case where he already redeemed before the investigation of price, he must complete the sum.

it has gone out to secular status to be sheared and worked. For a consecrated animal is forbidden to be sheared and worked, and after redemption it is permitted for this (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:7, 1:12; the preceding paragraph speaks of an altar-sacred animal that developed a blemish after being consecrated, which is forbidden to be sheared and worked even after redemption, ibid. halakhah 9).
three appraised it. Three expert appraisers on behalf of the Temple (as below 8:2).
that this is worth its price. That the secular animal is equal in value to the consecrated animal.
he does not return. There is no need to go back and make up the difference.
but if two appraised it. And this is not a proper appraisal, for consecrated items are appraised by three (ibid.).
that he deceived the Temple in any amount. That he misled the Temple even by a very small amount.
by estimate. By guess, without exact weighing and measuring.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 8.
the treasurers take it and are silent. Even though its value is more than the redemption and the fifth.
he completes the price as we explained. There.

for he redeemed at a fixed price. And he undertook to redeem at this sum and not less, and so even if there is a difference between what he said and the value of the consecrated item, he adds a fifth to the principal he stated.

and a second consecration does not require a fifth, as we explained. Above, halakhah 4. Although he redeemed at a fixed price, the cloak or the cow is not considered first consecration but second consecration, on whose redemption a fifth is not added.
he pulled it for a maneh. He pulled the consecrated item and undertook to give a hundred dinars for it.
until it stood at two hundred. The consecrated item's value rose to two hundred.

and gave the money and it stands for him. The verse's wording is: 'And he shall add a fifth of the money of your valuation to it and it shall be his' (Leviticus 27:19), and the quotation here follows the wording of the Tosefta, Arakhin 4:4 (according to the manuscript text and the first printing), and similarly in the Babylonian Talmud in several places (such as Berakhot 47b, Shabbat 128a; see Tosafot there, s.v. 've-natan ha-kesef').
by giving the money it is his. And so it was not acquired by him through pulling, and it turns out that it rose in value while in the Temple's possession.

the power of a layman shall not be stricter than the power of the Temple. And one who pulls from a layman acquires by pulling before giving the money (Hilchot Mekhirah 3:4; see also Hilchot Mekhirah 9:2).
and he acquired by pulling. And it turns out that the consecrated item became cheaper while in the redeemer's possession.

the power of a layman shall not be stricter than the power of the Temple. And with a layman the seller can retract and cancel the sale if the object rose in value after the money was given and before the buyer pulled (Hilchot Mekhirah 3:4).

until he accepts 'mi she-para'. As will be explained in its place, Hilchot Mekhirah 7:1-2, that although by law he may retract in such a case, it is not the act of Israel and he must receive 'mi she-para' like anyone who does not keep his word, whom the court curses with this formula: 'He who exacted payment from the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion... He will exact payment from one who does not stand by his word.'
and the Temple is not fit to receive 'mi she-para'. And therefore the Temple cannot retract and the redeemer receives it for a maneh.

and a woman's ketubah or creditors' bonds were against him. That he consecrated after he divorced his wife and did not pay her ketubah, or after he borrowed (and if he consecrated before he divorced, see below, halakhah 17).

for the consecration removes the prior lien. Unlike a pledged field that was sold to another, where the lien is still in force and the woman or the creditor can collect (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 19:3), consecration removes the lien (see also ibid. 18:7).
for her lien stands on this land. And when the field leaves the Temple's hand, the lien returns to force.

to two buyers etc.. In a case where the field pledged for the ketubah was sold to a buyer who sold it to another buyer, and the woman undertook to the first buyer not to collect her ketubah from his field, after the first buyer sold to the second buyer, she can collect her ketubah from the field, for she did not undertake to the second not to collect from him (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 19:8). Likewise in our case, after the field is redeemed from the Temple, the woman (or the creditor) may collect from the redeemer.

they first make the woman or creditor swear, as is the way of anyone who comes to collect from encumbered property. The lender must swear before taking from the encumbered property that the borrower did not already repay his debt and that it was not forgiven or sold to another (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 22:10).
as we explained. Above 4:27.

and he says, how much would a person give for this field in order to give the woman her ketubah and the creditor his debt. And if this sum is more than the ketubah or the debt, he pays the Temple the remainder, and pays the woman or creditor, and the field is his (Tiferet Yisrael, Arakhin 6:2).

and the buyer takes it even for a dinar so that they not say the Temple goes out without redemption. When the value of the field and the amount of the debt are equal, we do not say that he takes it from the Temple without payment for the woman or creditor to collect, lest they say that the Temple property goes out without redemption, and so he gives even one dinar. For this reason the woman or creditor themselves do not take directly from the Temple (even if they give the difference or a dinar to the Temple) lest they say the Temple goes out without redemption, for they take it directly in payment of the ketubah or the debt.

and even if the debt is a hundred and the field is worth ninety, on this basis one who wishes to redeem it redeems it. Although the redeemer must give the creditor the entire value of the field (ninety), he is not permitted to redeem without adding a dinar (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 6:2).

but if the debt was twice the field's price etc.. Since people can appraise the field at up to double its value, they might think the redemption covers both payment of the debt and a remainder designated for the Temple. But when the debt is double the price of the field, one cannot think so, and the concern returns that they will say the field is not redeemed at all (Kesef Mishneh; see Merkevet ha-Mishneh, who explained differently).

rather they redeem it in general terms, for if they stipulated to give, it is not redeemed at all. They redeem the field as an ordinary redemption, so that the redemption money goes to the Temple and the field belongs to the buyer, and there is no option to redeem by stipulating to give a dinar to the Temple and the field's value to the woman or creditor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arakhin 6:2).
and collected her ketubah. She came to collect her ketubah from the redeemed property (as above, halakhot 14-15).
until he vows her benefit. That her husband forbids himself benefit from her, which means he will never remarry her.
lest they colluded against the Temple. That they wished to trick the Temple in this way and collect the property (see also Hilchot Ishut 17:10).
and we do not say etc.. Although he has another way to get the consecration back for himself, by annulment of the vow (see Hilchot Nedarim 4:7), we do not rely on this and we suspect trickery.
this vessel belongs to so-and-so. That it had been deposited with me and I consecrated it.
lest they collude against the Temple. And so his fellow could collect his debt from the redeemer from the Temple.
he does not collect on this basis. The creditor cannot collect from the redeemer from the Temple on the basis of the borrower's statement alone.

rather in the way all creditors collect, as we explained. Above, halakhah 16, that he must swear that the borrower did not repay him the debt, and only afterward can the redeemer give him his debt from what he redeemed (as above, halakhah 16).
for a person does not scheme against the Temple... and sin for others. A person does not sin so that others will profit, such as his sons or heirs.

and he takes from the Temple because of the instruction. In both these cases he takes directly from the Temple on the basis of the borrower's statement, for when he says at the time of consecration 'a maneh of so-and-so is in my hand', his intention is that the consecration not take effect on this maneh (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).

we do not suspect him. Therefore if a person acquired property about which a rumor went out that it was declared ownerless, the court takes it from his hand and returns it to the owners. And when a rumor went out that he consecrated, we do not forbid him to use his property, and likewise it is permitted to have this property collected directly by a creditor without the need for the process of redemption.
all public needs. For example repairing damage to water, roads and streets, giving the sotah to drink, burning the red heifer and more (Hilchot Yom Tov 7:10, Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:1).
ready. Prepared.

with the terumah of the shekels. For these funds reach the Temple together with the half-shekel funds, which are also collected from the fifteenth of Adar (Hilchot Shekalim 1:9), and are used for public offerings and for other needs of the service and the building of the Temple (see ibid. chapter 4).
to strengthen the house of our God. For these funds are used for Temple repairs, its renovation and maintenance.
experts. Expert property appraisers.

when they collect movables that are taken as pledge from those liable for valuations. For a person who valued and cannot pay, his property is seized and sold, and the money is given to Temple repairs (above 3:14).
and when they value an animal and the like of other movables. That were consecrated for Temple repairs and are redeemed by giving their value to Temple repairs (above 5:3).

but when they value lands. For example if he consecrated a purchased field, whose law is that he gives its value to Temple repairs (above 4:26), and likewise one who consecrates a field of inheritance when the Jubilee is not in force (above 5:1; but when the Jubilee is in force it seems that ten are not needed, since its valuation is fixed in the Torah - see Tzafnat Pa'ne'ach).
if they were compelled to collect valuations of persons from his land. For example, he could not pay, and they seized his land in order to sell it and fund his obligation.

they are valued only by ten etc.. In the passage on valuations and consecrations the word 'kohen' (priest) appears ten times (Leviticus 27:8-23). Because the last time it was said regarding lands, the Sages learned that in the appraisal of lands, or in the appraisal of a person's worth (who is appraised as a slave sold in the market, and a slave is likened to lands - as above 7:1), ten are required, one of whom is a priest (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 23b; see Rashi there).
when they appraise him, how much he is worth or how much the worth of his hand or foot is. As above 1:9, 2:3.
they announce them before all who come to redeem. In a public auction.

they seize ten of his property. The difference between his offer and the offer before it, since he committed by his word to give, and if he does not give, the Temple will lose the consecrated item by this difference.
and they give the consecrated item to the one at thirty. So it turns out that the redeemer gave thirty, and the Temple took ten from the one who offered forty and ten from the one who offered fifty.
the first, who gave ten, retracted. So at the moment there is no redeemer.
they collect from the one at ten the remainder. For example if the redeemer gave five sela, they take five sela from the one who offered ten.
but if they all retracted at once, they divide among them equally. Since they retracted at once, they caused the Temple to lose the entire sum together, and so they divide it among them equally.

because they add a fifth. Since the owners add a quarter of the principal to the redemption sum (as above 4:5), in a case where the other offer is lower than or equal to this sum, the owners take precedence.
and they do not add a fifth to the increase of other redeemers etc.. The owners do not add a fifth to the added sum that others offered, but only in relation to what they originally offered.
and a fifth that they are liable for because of the fifth of the gift they gave at first. For they calculate the fifth relative to the original offer and not relative to the current offer.
and they added. The owners.

rather the fifth of what they gave at first they add to what the last one gave, if they wish. If the owners wish, they may add to the last bidder's offer, but they need not add a fifth to this offer but only to their original offer.
that he is worth what the last one gave. Who offered twenty-five sela.

and they give thirty-one and a dinar and a perutah. They give the twenty-five sela that the last one offered plus their fifth, which is six sela and a dinar, and they also give the perutah they added.
the last one came and gave twenty-six, he has priority. For he gave more than the principal and fifth the owners gave.
and if they wished and added even one perutah. That the owners added a perutah to his offer, so the offer now stands at twenty-six and a perutah.
they give thirty-one and a perutah. They give twenty-six and a perutah as they offered, and add five sela as a fifth relative to the original offer, which was twenty.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 5.
until it dies on its own. From hunger.
in the Great Sea, the Dead Sea. The Mediterranean, which is salty (unlike the Sea of Galilee).

a slave who entered the commandments. A Canaanite slave who was circumcised and immersed for the sake of slavery, and is considered to have partially converted and is obligated in commandments like women (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:11-12, Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).

and if he was a gentile slave, they neither raise nor lower. They do not lift him out and save him if he fell into a pit or other mortal danger, but they do not forcibly lower him into a pit or other mortal danger to kill him, as with any idol-worshiping gentile (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:1), and so here too he is not redeemed, nor is a door locked on him until he dies, but he is forbidden for benefit until he dies on his own (Radbaz; see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 9:14).
as we explained. Above 7:8.
one who in our time declared movables cherem in general terms. And the law of general cherem is for the priests (above 6:1).

for the cherem field applies only when the Jubilee is in force. As it is stated: 'And the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy to the Lord, like a field of cherem' (Leviticus 27:21), and from this, that the cherem field itself applies only in the Jubilee, as a field of inheritance (Babylonian Talmud, Arakhin 29a).
it is like movables in the Land of Israel. For the law of a cherem field is a commandment dependent on the Jubilee, and therefore it applies only in the Land of Israel.
miser. A stingy person.
there is nothing in that. And he has no sin.
and will need people. To collect donations from them.
destroyers of the world. Vessels of the world, who ruin a person's existence (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sotah 3:3).
rather, whoever scatters his money on commandments should not scatter more than a fifth. A fifth of his property (regarding charity see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 7:5).
that he bring according to his means. According to his financial ability.
